heading: MEMORANDUM to the President of Government
note: A memo with a fixed letterhead (blocks 6-11 are the running header, the word MEMORANDUM, To, From, Subject and Date, each measured as its own block) and then three moves: what the team built, what it found, what the government should do. The parameter summary (r1 risk, w individual benefit, b firm benefit, r2 punishment) is the paper's only compact statement of its own model, and it is given before any equation. The seven recommendations are ordinal prose in one bullet each and they map cleanly onto later chapters - no untradeable human right (3.1), suggested price by type (2.3-2.5), supervision and punishment (3.1), generational difference (3.3), quick action after a breach (3.4), a data-holder liability law (3.4), Pigovian tax or subsidy (4.2) - which makes this one of the few memos in the corpus that can be traced line by line. The memo is silent on the one thing the body admits twice: no sensitivity or robustness check was run.

heading: 1 Introduction (1.1 Background, 1.2 Statement of the problem)
note: The introduction spends two blocks on background that no later chapter uses (PI value is discussed, disclosure can harm the owner), then does the paper's real conceptual work in three blocks: PI is treated as a tradable item like public property and intellectual property, the transaction is a lease rather than a sale because the individual keeps ownership, and organisations may not resell. That leasing definition is load-bearing - it is what makes repeated transactions and the ownership caveat in the weaknesses section possible - and it is introduced here as an assumption, not argued. The restatement follows the standard move: define PI from the literature (a differentiation power, owned by the individual, not obtainable without permission), then announce AHP for risk, game theory for price, parameter manipulation for the extensions and graph theory for the network. The section does not state a research question; it states a pipeline, and blocks 54-56 are that pipeline plus the five-part outline. One block ([43]) is unusually long and mixes the policy motivation with the PP/IP analogy, which is why the argument there reads as compressed.

heading: 2.1 Assumptions
note: Six assumptions are crammed into one measured block (58) because the PDF interleaves the bullet list with the running prose, so the extraction sees one paragraph containing all six. They are: three sectors; individuals and organisations are self-interested market participants; PI sold to an organisation cannot be resold; a transaction is a bundle designed by the firm and accepted or refused by the individual; and the value of PI rises with the amount of information. Block 59 says the first four follow standard economic theory, block 60 justifies the sixth. The consequences are large and unstated: the no-resale rule removes arbitrage, and the bundle design by the firm means the individual never chooses which information to sell, only whether to sell the bundle. The second half of block 60 carries the 2.2 heading, so the notation section has no heading block of its own.

heading: 2.2-2.6 Base model (risk, cost-benefit, game, pricing power)
note: The core of the paper, five subsections each doing one job. 2.3 defines the risk r1 as a weighted sum of three sub-risks (marketing harassment, property loss, discrimination), each given a concrete monetary operationalisation: the harassment term is call time times wage, calibrated by asserting a 30-second call and a 200-unit daily wage gives r = 0.21; the fraud term uses the 9.9 CNY Alipay/ZhongTong insurance premium; the discrimination term is an indicator-vector inner product with a sensitivity-vector whose values the paper openly says 'needs further research'. Weights are then set by AHP from three hand-built reciprocal matrices, and the resulting vectors (0.45/0.10/0.45, 0.57/0.34/0.08, 0.20/0.31/0.49) are defended only by 'in accordance with our intuition'. The worked example gives r1 = 0.326. 2.4 turns the amount of information into x = C ln(n+1) with C the completeness ratio over 15 enumerated basic items, borrowed from the Wikipedia-completeness paper, and makes x the sole determinant of both b and w - the strongest simplification in the paper, later conceded in the weaknesses. 2.5 builds the two-period game: sell or not, then steal or not, with r2 the expected punishment; the sub-game perfect equilibrium yields P = one half of [(1-ps)b + (1+ps)r1] under two constraints, and the equal split is justified by citing Shapley, not by deriving the Shapley value. 2.6 reassigns pricing power: no market power gives a supply-demand crossing with a figure, the individual as price-setter gives P = (1-ps)(b+r2) with a quit branch, and both cases are read only through comparative statics on b and ps. Measurement merged the 18-row Table 1 into one group and split several paragraphs across page breaks; the running headers ('PI Pricing System Based on Game Theory and Graph Theory') are excluded throughout.

heading: 3 Application of our model (human right, timeliness, generations, breach)
note: Four applications, each a one-parameter perturbation of the base game, and each reaches a policy sentence rather than a number. 3.1 asks whether privacy is a human right and answers conditionally: when r1 is large and w small the market fails and the government should ban the trade, otherwise trade freely. It then does the paper's only genuine policy derivation - raising r2 until stealing is unprofitable, r2 > ps b/(1-ps), which the paper calls the supervision upper bound - and the resulting price P = one half of (b + r1 - w) is a real result, but the 'second method' declared optimal is chosen by assertion after a short comparison. 3.2 makes the amount of information decay: basic items change as a binomial process giving x(t) = x0 - lambda t, profitable items follow an exponential discount x0 exp(-ln2 t / h). The half-life h is never given a value, so the decay is never calibrated and the chapter ends with the qualitative point that old unsold data is a theft target - which is exactly what the memo repeats. 3.3 is the weakest application: the willingness-to-take-risk quartic f(x) is fitted from a figure with no stated data, mu = exp(-(p-5.1)/1.1) is a bijection invented from three stated constraints, and the only computed number, mu = 0.4678 at age 30, is produced by the fit rather than tested against anyone. 3.4 argues the massive-breach case through the same two equilibrium conditions: b falls, ps rises, r1 rises, the first condition fails and theft becomes rational, so regulation is needed; it cites US case law on damages and Acquisti on moral hazard, then closes with the counter-intuitive point that a breach can raise ps-protection effort and so improve welfare. The section is the only place where the model is applied to an event rather than a parameter.

heading: 4 Extension on network effect of PI
note: The extension moves from one individual to a population on a Barabasi-Albert scale-free graph of 10,000 nodes, generated in Python 2.7 and Matlab R2016b. The payoff is w_i - (1-ps)r_i - d and social utility adds a degree-weighted externality term e·v_i plus the tax revenue |I|d; w_i and r_i are drawn uniformly on [0,1], b = 0.1, ps = 0.05, e swept from -0.2 to 0.2 and d from -1 to 1 in steps of 0.01, and the optimal tax d_m is the argmax of U for each e. The results are read off Figures 5-8: the optimal tax is interior, it shifts left as e grows, U_max rises monotonically with e, and for negative externality the government can do little. This is the paper's only simulation with a grid and its only figure-based inference, and it is also where the Pigovian recommendation comes from. Two limits are visible and only one is admitted: the externality is assumed identical on every edge ('we assume that edge is identical'), so the network structure enters only through degree, and the 10,000-node draw is a single realisation with no replication. The closing block converts the result into a claim that the community need not protect citizens because the tax already compensates shared risk, which is a stronger statement than the simulation supports.

heading: 5.1 Strengths and weaknesses
note: Three claimed strengths and five admitted weaknesses, each a bullet split across blocks by the two-column-ish bullet layout. The strengths - a concise sequential game, parameters chosen by named methods (AHP, graph theory, psychological fitting), a scale-free simulation of externality - are all method claims with no result attached, and the second is the one the body undercuts, since the AHP weights are hand-set and mu is an invented bijection. The weaknesses are unusually honest and specific for this corpus: imperfect information is ignored, no robustness or sensitivity check was run for lack of data, the parameter forms are subjective, only one-to-one trade is modelled, and the cost of self-protection is omitted (with the ownership caveat that individuals can resell). The missing sensitivity analysis is the paper's real gap and the paper names it, which makes the memo's confident pricing recommendations harder to defend than the body admits. The '5.2 Conclusion' heading is glued to the tail of block 246.

heading: 5.2 Conclusion
note: Three blocks that restate the pipeline rather than the findings: a pricing system from game theory, the finding that selling PI can benefit both sides when government sets the price, then a paragraph per extension (human rights and supervision, timeliness, generational perception, network externality) and a closing sentence about the topic becoming hotter. No number is repeated from the body, no limitation is restated, and the network result is compressed into 'government can do little when the disclosure has negative externality' - the one sentence that is faithful to the simulation. The block boundary at 249 is the running header, not a paragraph, and the reference list starts immediately after block 250.
